_comment: Epilogues (issue #116): one short card per person at the ending (#32), read by scripts/epilogues.gd. cast: recruit id -> list of variants; the FIRST whose 'when' is met is used, and the last variant of each list must have no 'when' (the fallback; tests enforce it). People who never joined get no card; people lost on an expedition get their 'lost' variant. 'default' is used for anyone with no list of their own, so a new recruit always gets a card (add a list for them anyway: tests/test_relationships.gd lists who lacks one). {name} is the full name, {short} the short one. when keys (all must hold): romance ('partner' = with Ash at the end, 'ex' = it ended, 'friends' = Ash said no, 'none' = never asked), rank_min / rank_max (bond rank 0-5), personal ('done', 'open' = not done, 'lost' = not done and the Blank took the province), home ('held' / 'erased': their personal mission's province at the end), missions_min (missions fought with Ash), injuries_min (times hurt badly enough to be out of action), choice ({rank, pick}: which choice Ash made in that rank scene, 0 = first), lost (true = did not come back from an expedition), pair ({with, state}: state 'friends', 'rivals' or 'truce' with that person, who must have joined), betrayal (the climax betrayal fate, scripts/betrayal.gd: 'betrayed', 'redeemed' = taken back, 'let_go', 'faked' = Bran's con, 'none' = not involved).

bran.text: Bran sold Ash to the Vacancy for a price it could never pay, and walked out with the receipt. He had it framed. Every year Ash gets an invoice for one betrayal, faithfully performed, rates as agreed. At the bottom, in small print: "Offer still open. Better ones considered." The tattoo has not tightened since.

Brannoc Tolley never signed another contract. He trained the Hollowmark watch for no wage at all, which he complained about daily, and kept the forearm bare so the recruits could see the clean space where a name used to be. When they asked whose he was, he said, "Mine. Mostly. Some of it's on loan to a friend."

With his contract held by nobody, Bran found out what he was worth on the open market, and turned every offer down. He is still in Hollowmark, in the good chair, sending Ash an invoice every year for one river-drowned pen. It has never been paid. It never will be. That is the point.

Bran went back to selling his axe, honestly this time, with the terms read aloud. He still visits Mother Gristle every winter to settle up. She still overcharges him. He pays without a word, and they both pretend it's about the money.
When the work dried up, Bran sold his axe to a caravan company on the Tithe Road and told everyone he'd kept a clause for himself: if Ash ever sends word, he walks. They laughed. He meant it.

Brannoc Tolley collected his last wage and left on the first barge out, still owned by a man he never met. Somewhere downriver, they say, the contract tightened one more time, at a better offer. He told the new client first. Then he left.

gristle.text: Mother Gristle's name stayed on the Coven tree, carved deep. She took the elder's chair Hester Vane left empty and ran the Gutterwoods like a clinic: everybody seen, everybody billed. She never once collected from the poor. She just never told anyone that, either.

Mother Gristle went back to the Gutterwoods with her name on the tree and her ledger clean for the first time in forty years. It lasted a week. Then someone needed stitching, and she opened a new page, and wrote Ash's name at the top of it, just to keep her hand in.

Mother Gristle kept the Infirmary until the beds emptied, then sold it back to Hollowmark at a scandalous mark-up. She lives on the edge of the swamp now. People still come. She still bills them. She still saves them.
Mother Gristle left with her bottles and a sack of unpaid invoices. Hollowmark still owes her eleven Gilt, four coppers and one life. She says she'll be back to collect. Nobody doubts it.

ninefingers.text: Daro came back and asked for a court-martial. Hollowmark didn't have one, so Daro wrote the charges out, read them aloud on the plaza and served the sentence: a year of latrine duty at the Barracks. They did every day of it. The recruits still talk about how clean those latrines got.

Ash let Daro go. They walked east where the Tithe Road turns to paper, toward a village with their name on its memorial plaque. Some say the Vacancy kept its word and Hob's Wick stands out there, unstruck. Some say Daro is still walking. The Barracks keep their bunk made, corners square.

Corporal Daro stayed dead, officially, which made it very difficult to marry them. Ash managed it anyway, in the chapel at Hob's Wick, under their own memorial plaque. The goats attended. Forty villagers wept for a hero who stood at the altar, very much alive, and told them all to stop that at once.

Daro went back to Hob's Wick and took up the mill. They kept a seat at the long table for Ash, empty, every harvest. Nobody asked who it was for. Daro would only have said, "A soldier I served with," and changed the subject to beer.

Corporal Daro, fallen against the Blank, still gets prayed for every week in Hob's Wick. They live two doors down from the chapel under another name and never correct anyone. Once a year a letter arrives from Hollowmark addressed to the plaque. They always answer it.

Daro never did find out if Hob's Wick survived. The road there went white before they could look. They drilled the Barracks recruits until there was no one left to drill, then walked off east one morning, alone, toward where the village used to be.

Daro took over the Barracks for good. They taught three hundred recruits how to watch a back, and one rule above all: if the order's wrong, tear it up. Nine fingers, every one of them pointed at you while they said it.

Daro left the way they joined the Concord: in the middle of the night, with a bag over one shoulder and a poster with ten fingers on it. Nobody saw where they went. Nobody looked very hard. They'd made sure of that.

quill.text: Quill and Odile Penhallow opened a counting-house in Hollowmark that keeps only honest books. It loses money every year. They argue about the rounding every night. Thirty-one names hang framed above the door, carried forward, and one more below them that won't stay in ink: ASH. Balanced.

Edwin Pask kept Hollowmark's books until the day he died, one true set, no beautiful ones. The thirty-one stayed carried forward. The last page of his last ledger is blank except for one line at the bottom, in his best hand: ASH. Balanced.
Quill went on cooking the books, for the town this time instead of the Concord. Every year the numbers came out in Hollowmark's favour, by a margin so small no auditor could ever find it. Many tried.

Edwin Pask went back to the Concord with both sets of books under his arm and asked for his old post. They gave it to him. Nobody knows which set he handed in. He has never said, and he looks very tired.

tobble.text: Old Tobble never retired. The Last Drop's sign hangs over the tavern door in Hollowmark, cracked and gilt, and he pours under it every night, complaining about his knees. There is a stool at the end of the bar nobody else is allowed to sit on. The second drink on it is always free.

Tobble announced his retirement the week after it was all over, and has announced it every week since. Quill keeps a running tally on the tavern wall. It is the only tab in Hollowmark that has never been disputed.
Tobble finally retired. It lasted nine days. On the tenth he was back behind the bar, because, as he put it, somebody has to know where the good barrel is, and it isn't going to be one of you.

Old Tobble sold the tavern to a Guild man and retired to the Meadow, to a roof that wasn't there any more, by a sign he never went back for. He was found every evening by the edge of the white with two mugs, one full.

abeyance.text: Sister Hild never went back to the Abbey. The voices stayed quiet as long as someone was holding her hand, so someone usually was. She kept the slip of paper in a locket, NOT YET, and checked it every morning. It never changed. She took that as a promise kept.

Sister Hild founded a small scriptorium in the Wickham Hills, in the chapel where her page found its book. Its scribes copy nothing; they listen. Every novice is given a slip of paper on their first day. On it, in her famous serifs: NOT YET.

The page drew its map one more time, toward a chapel the Blank had already taken, then went blank and stayed that way. Sister Hild kept it anyway. She says the voices are quieter now. She doesn't say whether that frightens her.

Sister Hild stayed on in the Scriptorium long after there was anything left to research. She was found most nights asleep at her desk with the page under her cheek, and in the mornings there were always new lines on it. She never let anyone read them.

Sister Hild slipped away one night with her stolen page, the way she had left the Abbey. A rumour says she went back to them. Another says the Abbey went looking for her and found only polite voices. Both rumours are probably true.

ottoline.text: Ottoline walked out of the Margin behind Ash and took the Hollowmark gate without being asked. She never mentions the deal. Once a year she hands Ash a coat-check ticket, number seven, and Ash hands it back. The coat tree in the plaza has a seventh peg now. Nobody hangs anything on it.

Ash let Ottoline go into the white with the Vacancy's half-kept promise. Ferrymen at the Gallows crossing say there's a door out there now, standing on nothing, and a big woman in front of it who lets nobody through. At closing she counts to six. Then, after a while, to seven.

Big Ottoline opened a new Crimson Encore on the Hollowmark plaza. No closing duel; the closing act is her throwing out the last drunk, to applause. Ash's name is painted at the top of the door frame in gold, where everyone can see it. Nobody has ever been stupid enough to ask about it twice.

Ottoline kept the door at Tobble's for twenty years. Every closing time she stacked the chairs alone, two at a time, then three. If Ash came in, she'd bar the door behind them without a word, so nobody could interrupt. Then she'd go and sit at the other end of the room.

Six coats still hang on the old tree in the plaza; Ottoline won't let anyone take them down. She keeps Hollowmark's gate now, and she has a list in chalk on the gatepost, as long as her arm. Strangers are on it in chalk. Ash is on it in ink.

The knocking on Lantern Row stopped when the Blank took Gallows Ferry. Ottoline never found out who it was. She still carries six coat-check tickets tied with red ribbon, and every night, at the door, she counts to six before she shuts it.
Ottoline went back to doors, any door that would pay. Taverns, banks, once a cathedral. She never lets anyone through who shouldn't be there, and never shuts one while anyone is still on the stairs.
Big Ottoline went off to keep a door in Gallows Ferry and was never short of work. They say she still stands in front of it at closing time a moment too long, listening, before she shuts it.

jessamy.text: Jessamy Leake, occupation: yes, next of kin: Ash. She still runs freight, by day now, wearing an enormous hat she won't say where she got. She and Ash live above a warehouse full of crates nobody asks about. Every noon, without fail, she drags Ash out onto the roof to lie in the sun.

Jessamy went back to working nights, by choice this time. She is the best smuggler in the Inklands and charges Hollowmark exactly nothing, which annoys her more than she lets on. She sends Ash a pear every autumn. No note. You don't need a note with a pear.

Jessamy Leake is in the Ledger now, solid from noon to midnight, sunburnt every summer and delighted about it. She runs the best freight company on the Tithe Road and declares every crate. Honestly. Mostly. Her crates say "occupation: yes" on the side.

The Tithe Road went white before Jessamy could make the notary write her back in. She went on fading, a little more each year. The last anyone saw of her she was sitting on a Hollowmark roof at dawn, waiting for the light, smiling like she'd finally worked out how to steal it.

Jessamy kept smuggling, and kept fading, and kept laughing about it. She sends Hollowmark one crate a month, unlabelled. It is always exactly what the town is short of. Nobody has ever caught her delivering it.

Jessamy left the way she worked: after dark, without a word, with a crate nobody saw her take. A few years later there were stories on the coast about a smuggler you could see the sea through. She never came back to Hollowmark. It was too bright.

odile.text: Odile came back and entered the whole affair in her own ledger: one betrayal, under Liabilities, carried forward. She pays it down a line at a time. Every quarter Ash gets a statement, initialled, the balance a little smaller. She has asked, in writing, that it never be written off.

Ash let Odile go to her mother's house at the Old Mill, or whatever the Vacancy wrote back of it. Letters come from there sometimes in Penhallow red ink, about nothing: the weather, a rounding error. They are never signed. Quill files them under Correspondence, Pending.

Odile Penhallow kept the Inklands' honest books and Ash's heart in the same ledger, in red ink, under Assets, jointly held. Her mother came to the wedding and audited the catering. It balanced. Marguerite Penhallow cried, briefly, which she then billed to herself.

Odile became the first Assessor of the free provinces and the fairest one anyone had ever met. In the back of her private ledger there is one line written off, never struck through. She has never explained it, and nobody who has seen her face has asked.

Odile Penhallow audited every Concord ledger she could get her hands on, and found every village they had meant to sell. Every one of them got very, very expensive. She signs her reports with a pen her mother gave her and initials one copy for Ash, every time.

Odile and Daro finished their list. It had forty-one names on it. Odile assessed each one for back taxes; Daro delivered the bills, in person. Nobody on the list has ever been seen in the Inklands again. They are, technically, all paid up.
Odile went back to collecting. Taxes, this time, for the free provinces, a fair tenth and not a copper more. She once fined a governor for rounding up. People still talk about it in awe.

Odile Penhallow took the stolen ledger and left Hollowmark for her mother's house. Nobody knows what passed between them. The ledger was never seen again, and neither, in the Inklands, was a Penhallow collector.

velvette.text: Fauvette retired from the stage at the height of her fame and wrote her memoirs, which named everyone. Chapter nine is about a silent stagehand and is considered the most romantic thing ever printed in the Inklands. She will not say who it's about. Everyone knows. She calls Ash by a very ordinary name, when nobody's listening.

Fauvette went back on the stage and played every lover in the repertoire, and in every one of them, for one beat in the third act, she looked up at the wings. Critics called it her finest touch. She said it was a draught, darling, and refused to discuss it.

Augustin Sallow lived, as Ash asked, and stood trial with his own receipts pinned to his coat. Fauvette testified in costume. Afterwards she opened a theatre where the closing act is a reading of eleven names, every night, and the audience takes off its hats.

Fauvette gave her last performance on the Gilded Heron and never gave another. She runs the best salon in the Inklands now, where every secret is still for sale, except one. Ash keeps that one. Nobody else will ever hear it.

The Saltreed went white with the Gilded Heron still on it, and Augustin Sallow with it, and his receipts. Fauvette never got her last performance. She went back on stage anyway, and in the closing act she reads eleven names nobody else can check, and the audience doesn't know why it's crying.
Fauvette went back to the stage, and to her little book of secrets, and was magnificent in both. Every faction in the Inklands is terrified of her. She's very proud of that.

Fauvette took the first good offer: a new theatre, a new stage name, a new book of other people's secrets. Somewhere in it there's an entry about Hollowmark. It's short. She charges a great deal for it.

pell.text: Pell Mossop went into the white and did not come back. Back in Hollowmark there was a grave ready for them, dug with care, the right length. Nobody has ever found out who dug it.
Pell and Sister Hild keep the Hollowmark graveyard together. Pell digs; Hild listens. The dead have a lot to say about the new arrangements. Most of it is complimentary.
Pell went on digging graves before anyone died. In the years after, fewer and fewer of them were needed. Pell found this professionally disappointing, and personally a great relief.

hesper.text: Hetty Coyne mapped the way out of the white before she went in. The others followed it home. She didn't. Her last map hangs in the Command room: every road correct, and one small figure, drawn at the edge, walking off the page.
Hetty Coyne drew the first true map of the Inklands after the Blank. It is a week out of date in the wrong direction, and is the most accurate map in the world.

dunmore.text: Dunmore Vellacott walked into the white with every debt he owed written on his skin. The Blank took the lot. Somewhere a great many creditors are still waiting at a great many gates.

Dunmore Vellacott paid off his last debt, the one on his left heel, five years after it was all over. Odile Penhallow stamped it PAID, in red. He has had the stamp tattooed over every single entry, and wears short sleeves now, in all weathers.
Dunmore Vellacott kept working the forge and paying his debts down, a forearm a year. He has started tattooing the paid ones with little flowers. He says he's nearly a garden.

osyth.text: Sister Osyth went into the white with her board on its string. The squad that came back said she was counting out loud the whole way in. The last number they heard was a new one.

Sister Osyth finished her count, then started again from one, to check. The Abbey carved the total over the Founders' Door: eleven thousand four hundred and six. She had them chisel it twice, because the first mason rounded.

nell.text: Nell Tapper went out with a lantern into the white and did not come back. Candleford still keeps a candle in every window all night. Now everyone knows who for.

Nell Tapper still runs Candleford and the chandlery, still two jobs, now with wages. The Abbey pays on time. She keeps the receipt for the first payment framed over the counter, next to the one for the five barges she was never paid for.

cuthbert.text: Brother Cuthbert walked into the white ringing his hand-bell. They heard it for a long time afterwards. Some pilgrims at Scarth Pass say they still do, on clear nights, on the hour.

Brother Cuthbert went back up to Saint Ledger's and rang the tenor bell, one hour at a time, for the rest of his life. He never heard a note of it. He said he could feel when it was right, in his teeth.

alcuin.text: Brother Alcuin went into the white still wearing the Eraser coat with one sleeve. He told the squad he had read enough drafts to know where it ended. He did not come back to say if he was right.

Brother Alcuin sewed the sleeve back on in the end, and then took the coat off. He keeps the Abbey's new library, where the unedited drafts sit on the shelves next to the Ledger, both open, and anyone may read either.

biscuits.text: Mr. Biscuits went into the white barking and was not seen again. Sometimes, on still nights at the edge of the Blank, there is a sound like someone very far off saying "walkies". The Coven leaves a biscuit out, just in case.

Mr. Biscuits went back to the Coven with a medal on his collar and a reputation. Whether he is a dog that walks like a man or a man under a very old curse remains unsolved. He has stopped caring. He has a very good basket.

merrow.text: The Merrow Three went into the white singing, in three parts, and it held its breath for them. Then they were gone. Some nights in the margins you can still hear the harmony, a fourth part where there should be three.

The Merrow Three and Fauvette toured the free provinces with the Encore's old closing number, four voices, one spotlight. Pim got the high bit every night. Posy has started speaking to her again. Pet still doesn't need to.
The Merrow Three still share one voice, passed round like a hot coal. They sing in the margins wherever the white once was, and the land, slowly, remembers the tune.

default.text: {name} went into the white with the squad and did not come back. Their name is on the wall in Hollowmark, with the others. The white gave nothing back.
{name} stayed on in Hollowmark when it was over. Ask about the old days and {short} will tell you, at length, that they were there for all of it.

hortense.text: Hortense de Saulx gave up the masquerade and threw one party a year in Hollowmark, which the whole Causeway now rows across the lake for. She hosts it with Ash, and tells everyone it is a political arrangement. She has told nobody the truth about it except Ash, and she never lies to Ash.

Hortense went back to the Causeway and became the most sought-after hostess in the Inklands. Every year she sends Hollowmark an invitation addressed to the person who does not exist, and Guests. It is never answered. It is always sent.

Bérénice de Saulx grew up to run the Causeway's first school where the daughters of debtors learn to read contracts instead of copy them. Her sister teaches deportment, fencing and lying, and is very good at all three. The marquise says she has one true friend, and does not name them, and does not have to.

The Vauclair Terraces went white with the Office's school still on them. Hortense never spoke of her sister again. She went on dancing, beautifully, and the Causeway never noticed that she had stopped counting.
Hortense went home to the Causeway and charmed the new council into existence, then into doing what she wanted. Nobody is entirely sure which side she is on. She likes it that way.

Hortense de Saulx left one morning with a borrowed horse and a stolen map, and was reported, over the next ten years, at every court and masquerade in the Inklands, under nine names. All of them were lies. All of them were her.

saffron.text: Saffron Kiss finished every song she ever started after Hollowmark, and none of them went away. The love song is the one everybody asks for. She only sings it to one person, at the front, in the best seat.
Saffron went back on the bill and wrote the saddest song in the Inklands, about a quiet sort. She finished it. People cried on three Causeway bridges at once. She was very pleased with that.

Maud Pickering opened a music hall on the Pendower Shallows, on the moorings where the Mary Rudd used to lie. Her mam runs the bar. Every song she sings there is finished, and the hall is the warmest building on the lake.

The Shallows went white with the sung house still standing on them. Saffron never got to the last verse. She still sings, and stops before the end of every song, and the lights in a window that isn't there go on and off over the lake.
Saffron Kiss went back to the Causeway cabarets and topped every bill. She sings a song about Hollowmark mud that has a different ending every night, because she still has not chosen one.
Saffron took a contract with a showboat and sang her way down every river in the Inklands. Bargemen say that on still nights you can see a bridge across the water that only lasts as long as the song.

nan.text: Nan Cripps went straight, more or less. She runs a card room in Hollowmark where the games are honest because her shadow deals. Tally keeps the contract in his pocket, which is a trick nobody has worked out, and tells every customer the odds before they sit down.

Nan kept her own contract in her own strongbox and her shadow out in the open, talking. She became the Inklands' most trusted grifter, which she says is a contradiction, and which Tally says is the only honest thing about her.

Lantern Quay went white with Old Pratt's strongbox in it, and the contract, and then one morning Tally was gone with them. Nan still talks to her shadow sometimes. It does not answer. She does not cheat at cards any more, and she does not know why.
Nan Cripps sold the Concord a bridge across the Blank and spent the proceeds on rebuilding Hollowmark's market. Tally signed the receipt. The Concord is still trying to find the bridge.
Nan took her share and left by the back door, with three decks of cards and somebody else's horse. Tally sent a letter a month later apologising for the horse. Nan did not sign it.

ilse.text: Dame Ilse of the Mirror never went back into the glass. She hung the town hall mirror in the house she shared with Ash, and in it, every morning, there were two people, the right way round.

Ilse went back to the coast and took up the old Kernick post on the headland. She kept a mirror in every room and stood in front of each of them alone, and the tenants said she looked magnificent and a little lost.
Ilse held Kernick Head in her own name. The tenants call her the Dame and do not ask which one. The gallery has forty new mirrors, and in every one of them she moves first.

The white took Kernick Head with the gallery still in it. Ilse never looked into the last mirror. She still checks every morning that she is in front of the glass and not behind it, and one morning she was not there to check.

Ilse rode the coast road as its knight, which nobody had asked for and everybody came to expect. She stops at every chapel to fix her hair in the glass. She is never late, and she is never the wrong way round.

Ilse left Hollowmark for the capital, where the mirrors are the biggest in the Inklands. Somebody saw her in the Spire's hall of glass, admiring herself, and swore that her reflection was a beat behind.

kerra.text: Kerra Hocking dived every wreck on the coast and brought up the name board of every boat the white had taken. The families hung them in Trevail chapel. There is room left on the wall, and she means to fill it.
Kerra went home to Polgarrow and kept the light with her father. She writes his five lost days in the margin of every log, small, so that somebody does.

yann.text: Yann Le Goff sold Halfwave salt in every market in the Inklands and got rich on it. The salt from the year the sea stopped fetches the most. A pinch of it on the tongue, the label promises, brings back the taste of a day you have lost.
Yann went back to the pans at Halfwave and sold salt to the Moot at a fair price, which nobody on the coast will believe.

anselme.text: Anselme Brugière kept the old presses running on the Vauclair Terraces, and the year after the Blank was driven back the wine tasted of grapes again. He named the vintage after Hollowmark. It is terrible. He is very proud of it.

margot.text: Margot Vasseur stopped making masks and started making faces: portraits of everyone who came home from the war with the Blank, so there would be a record nobody could strike out. She made one of Ash. It is the only picture of the person who does not exist.

gaspard.text: Gaspard Pellerin went back to the Shallows when the ink fell, and the nets came up full of ordinary words again: 'bread', 'tomorrow', 'perhaps'. He sold them cheap to anyone who had run out.
